introduction_markdown: GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0755 Geology 1, JUNE 2019, ADVANCED LEVEL. Multiple choice question paper, one and a half hours. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room. Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil throughout the examination; do not open the booklet until told to do so; check that the booklet is headed "0755 GEOLOGY 1 - ADVANCED LEVEL"; fill in the information required on the answer sheet (Candidate Name, Exam Session, Subject Code and Candidate Identification Number). Answer ALL the 50 questions. All questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate, find the number of the question on the answer sheet and draw a horizontal line across the letter to join the square brackets for the answer you have chosen. Mark only one answer for each question: if you mark more than one answer you will score a zero for that question. Avoid spending too much time on any one question; you can come back to it later. Do all rough work in the booklet using the blank spaces. At the end of the examination the invigilator collects the answer sheet first and then the question booklet.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of these two gases are the most dominant in space?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The universe is made almost entirely of the two lightest elements. Hydrogen makes up roughly 74 % of the ordinary (visible) matter by mass and helium about 24 %, because both were formed in the Big Bang and are the fuel and product of the nuclear fusion that powers stars. Oxygen and carbon are far less abundant, as they are only made later inside stars. The only option that pairs the two most abundant gases is C.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Why does planet Mars lack plate tectonic activities?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Plate tectonics is driven by heat escaping from the interior (mantle convection), which moves and recycles the plates. Mars is much smaller than the Earth, so it lost its internal heat quickly; its interior is now cold and its lithosphere is thick and rigid, so the crust cannot break into plates that move and are recycled. Mars does have a mantle (B is false) and a lithosphere (D is false), and option A only restates the effect (the absence of plate recycling) instead of giving the reason. The best printed reason is C (strictly, Mars has very little remaining internal heat rather than none).

**Answer: C.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown:
The geologic process that actually explains the splitting of landmasses is:

*Options as printed:* A) Continental drift   B) Plate Tectonics   C) Seafloor spreading   D) Rifting
questions.corrige_markdown:
Continental drift (Wegener, 1912) only described the fact that the continents have moved apart; it was rejected for decades because it gave no mechanism. The theory that actually explains why and how landmasses split is **plate tectonics**: the lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that are moved by mantle convection and slab pull, so that a continent is stretched, rifted and finally split, with new ocean floor created by sea floor spreading. Sea floor spreading and rifting are stages or parts of this process, not the overall explanation.

**Intended answer: B (Plate Tectonics).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: A record of earthquake waves at a seismic station is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The seismometer is the sensor that detects the ground motion, the seismograph is the complete recording instrument, and seismology is the science of earthquakes. The trace (the record) drawn by the instrument, showing the arrival of the P, S and surface waves, is a **seismogram**.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the name given to the layer of the Earth at depth of between 100km and 350km where P and S wave velocities suddenly drop?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Below the rigid lithosphere (about 0 to 100 km) the upper mantle is close to its melting point and partially molten, weak and plastic. Seismic waves slow down there, which gives the **low velocity zone** at about 100 to 350 km. This layer is the asthenosphere. The outer core is at 2 900 km depth and is where S waves stop altogether, and the mantle is a much thicker and more general unit.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which property of a rock controls the velocity of P waves?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The speed of seismic waves depends on the elastic properties (rigidity and incompressibility) and on the density of the material through which they travel. Of the properties listed, density is the one that is used to explain velocity differences between rocks, for example the faster P waves in the dense peridotite of the mantle compared with the lighter granite of the crust. Texture and competence (the resistance of a bed to folding) do not control wave speed in the same direct way, and composition acts mainly through the density.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Why are there more frequent earthquakes in Japan than in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Most earthquakes happen where plates meet and move against each other. Japan lies on the convergent boundaries where the Pacific and Philippine Sea plates subduct beneath the Eurasian and North American plates, so strain is released very often. Cameroon lies in the interior of the African plate, far from any plate boundary, so large earthquakes are rare. B states exactly this contrast. A and C only describe Japan, and D is false because Cameroon has faults and the Cameroon Volcanic Line, but they are not at a plate boundary.

**Answer: B.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the composition of the upper mantle?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The upper mantle is made of ultramafic rock, mainly **peridotite** (olivine and pyroxene). Granite is the typical rock of the continental crust, basalt makes the oceanic crust and dolerite is a medium grained rock of the same composition as basalt, found in dykes and sills.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram below (Figure 1) to answer questions 9 and 10.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: a six-sided (hexagonal) prism with the prism faces marked a, b and c.*

How many crystallographic axes does this model have?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The model is a hexagonal prism. Crystals of the **hexagonal system** are described with **four** crystallographic axes: three equal horizontal axes ($a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$) at $120^\circ$ to each other in one plane and a fourth axis, $c$, perpendicular to that plane (the length of the prism). Three axes describe the cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic and monoclinic or triclinic systems.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use the diagram below (Figure 1, the same hexagonal prism as in question 9) to answer this question.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: a hexagonal prism.*

Name a mineral that crystallizes in this habit.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The habit shown is a six-sided prism, which belongs to the hexagonal system. **Beryl** ($\mathrm{Be_3Al_2Si_6O_{18}}$) crystallizes in the hexagonal system, in long six-sided prisms. Zircon and idocrase (vesuvianite) are tetragonal, and staurolite is orthorhombic (pseudo-monoclinic, often in cross shaped twins).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the most common form exhibited by the micas?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Micas (muscovite, biotite) have a perfect basal cleavage, so they occur as thin elastic sheets or flakes that peel off in layers, which is the **foliated** (platy or micaceous) habit. Fibrous habit is typical of asbestos, acicular (needle-like) of natrolite or tourmaline, and tabular of feldspars and barite. Individual mica crystals can also be described as tabular, but foliated is the form usually quoted for the group.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the minerals below is a common polymorph of $\mathrm{TiO_2}$?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Polymorphs have the same chemical formula but different crystal structures. $\mathrm{TiO_2}$ occurs as **rutile** (the commonest), anatase and brookite. Tridymite is a polymorph of $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, and kyanite and andalusite are polymorphs of $\mathrm{Al_2SiO_5}$.

**Answer: B.**

*Table 1*

Specimens W and Y which are both present in granite, can be identified respectively as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
W has hardness 7 and a conchoidal fracture with no cleavage: this is **quartz**. Y has a perfect basal cleavage and is black: this is **biotite**, the dark mica of granite (muscovite is colourless to silvery). Orthoclase (hardness 6, two cleavages at about $90^\circ$) is specimen X, not Y. Option D is less precise: biotite is a mica, but the black colour identifies the particular mica.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the table below (Table 1, as in question 13) and answer this question.

| Specimen | Description |
|---|---|
| W | Hardness 7, fracture conchoidal. |
| X | Hardness 6, 2 cleavage planes |
| Y | Basal cleavage, black colour |
| Z | SG 3.3, lustre glassy, colour green |

*Table 1*

Specimen X is a feldspar formed at high temperature, present in basalt. What is X?
questions.corrige_markdown:
X (hardness 6 with two cleavage planes) is a feldspar. The plagioclase of **basalt** is calcium rich, of intermediate to calcic composition, typically **labradorite** (about $\mathrm{An_{50\text{-}70}}$). Sodic plagioclase (albite, oligoclase) forms at lower temperature in acid rocks such as granite and syenite, while bytownite and anorthite are the very calcic members found mainly in gabbro and anorthosite.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the following minerals: calcite, olivine, sillimanite, orthoclase, quartz and labradorite. Use the above information to answer questions 15 and 16.

Which of these minerals occur in both sedimentary and metamorphic rocks?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Calcite** is in limestone (sedimentary) and marble (metamorphic). **Quartz** is in sandstone and in quartzite, schist and gneiss. **Orthoclase** is in arkose (sedimentary) and in gneiss (metamorphic). Olivine and labradorite are minerals of basic igneous rocks, and sillimanite is found in metamorphic rocks only, so A, B and D each contain a mineral that fails the test.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the following minerals: calcite, olivine, sillimanite, orthoclase, quartz and labradorite. Use this list to answer the question.

Which of these minerals occur only in metamorphic rocks?
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Sillimanite** ($\mathrm{Al_2SiO_5}$) is an index mineral of high temperature metamorphism of aluminium-rich rocks (pelites). Labradorite, olivine and orthoclase are all typical minerals of igneous rocks (labradorite and olivine of basalt and gabbro, orthoclase of granite).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two igneous rocks E and F were collected during field work. The minerals of E could be identified with the naked eye and the rock was light in colour. The minerals of F could not be identified with the naked eye and were dark in colour. Use these statements to answer questions 17, 18 and 19.

What is the environment of formation of F?
questions.corrige_markdown:
F is very fine grained (its minerals cannot be seen without a lens) and dark: this is a basic extrusive rock such as basalt. Fine grains mean fast cooling, which happens at the surface, so the environment is **volcanic**. A plutonic rock would be coarse grained and a hypabyssal rock (in dykes and sills) would be medium grained. A hot spot is a source of magma, not a rock-forming environment.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two igneous rocks E and F were collected during field work. The minerals of E could be identified with the naked eye and the rock was light in colour. The minerals of F could not be identified with the naked eye and were dark in colour. Use these statements to answer questions 17, 18 and 19.

What was the condition that led to the formation of E?
questions.corrige_markdown:
E has crystals large enough to be seen with the naked eye (coarse grained) and is light coloured (rich in quartz and feldspar): it is a plutonic rock such as granite. Large crystals grow only when the magma cools **slowly** at depth. Options C and D speak of lavas, which are erupted at the surface and cool quickly, so they cannot describe a coarse grained intrusive rock.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Two igneous rocks E and F were collected during field work. The minerals of E could be identified with the naked eye and the rock was light in colour. The minerals of F could not be identified with the naked eye and were dark in colour. Use these statements to answer questions 17, 18 and 19.

The textures of the two rocks are respectively:
questions.corrige_markdown:
E has visible minerals, so it is **coarse grained** (phaneritic); F has minerals that cannot be seen with the naked eye, so it is **fine grained** (aphanitic). Taken in the order E then F, the answer is coarse then fine. The wording of the statement does not suggest a medium grained (porphyritic or hypabyssal) rock.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the factor that controls the stability of minerals in a rock during weathering?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Goldich showed that the order of stability of minerals at the surface is the same as Bowen's reaction series read the other way round. Minerals that crystallized at the **highest temperature** (olivine, calcic plagioclase, pyroxene) are the farthest from equilibrium with surface conditions and weather first, while those formed at the lowest temperature (muscovite, quartz) are the most stable. Pressure, pore fluids and the overall rock composition influence the rate of weathering, but the factor that ranks the stability of the minerals themselves is their temperature of formation.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Why will shale be more susceptible to contact metamorphism than sandstone?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Shale is made of clay minerals and other fine, hydrous and chemically reactive minerals (rich in Al, Fe, Mg and K), which recrystallize easily into new minerals such as andalusite, cordierite and biotite and give hornfels. Sandstone consists mainly of quartz, which is chemically stable over a wide range of temperature, so it only recrystallizes to quartzite and shows little change. The difference comes from the **composition**; colour has no effect and grain size or bedding structures are secondary.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The description of two metamorphic rocks G and H is as follows: G is coarse grained and contains quartz and micas while H is medium grained and contains chlorite and micas. Use this statement to answer questions 22 and 23.

G and H are respectively:

*Options as printed:* A) Schist and phyllite   B) Phyllite and slate   C) Gneiss and schist   D) Slate and schist
questions.corrige_markdown:
A rock made of quartz and micas that is coarse enough to show its flakes and has a wavy foliation is a **schist** (G). A rock whose main minerals are chlorite and fine micas (sericite), with a silky sheen and a finer grain, is a **phyllite** (H), the grade between slate and schist. A gneiss (option C) would be banded and would contain feldspar as well, which the description of G does not mention. Options B and D put slate (very fine grained, no visible minerals) in the wrong place.

**Intended answer: A (Schist and phyllite).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The description of two metamorphic rocks G and H is as follows: G is coarse grained and contains quartz and micas while H is medium grained and contains chlorite and micas. Use this statement to answer questions 22 and 23.

State the type of metamorphism that produced both rocks.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Foliated rocks such as phyllite and schist form over large areas under directed pressure and rising temperature during mountain building, which is **regional** metamorphism. Contact metamorphism gives non-foliated hornfels around an intrusion and dynamic metamorphism gives crushed fault rocks. (Dynamothermal is another name for regional metamorphism, but "regional" is the standard term.)

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 2) and answer questions 24 and 25.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: a layered sequence in which the layer called bed x flows in curved lines around separate, lens shaped bodies of the layer called bed y.*

What type of bed is labelled X?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the diagram the layer y has been broken into separate lenses (boudins) while the layer x bends and flows around them. The layer that flows plastically is the weak, **incompetent** bed; the layer that breaks into blocks is the strong, competent bed. Limestones and sandstones name rocks, not the type of behaviour, so they cannot be right.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 2, the same diagram as in question 24) and answer this question.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: the layer bed x flows around lens shaped bodies of the layer bed y.*

A rock type that may represent rock Y is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Bed y is the competent layer that broke into lenses (boudinage), so it is a strong, brittle rock. Of the choices, **quartzite** (a hard rock made of quartz) is the one that is competent and bedded. Mudstone is weak and incompetent (it would behave like bed x), granite is a massive igneous rock and not a bed, and hornfels is a contact metamorphic rock that is not found as a layer in a folded sequence.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 3) and answer questions 26 and 27.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: a block diagram showing an anticline at the left end of the block, cut by a fault whose plane is vertical on the front face, with the left side marked by a downward arrow and the right side by an upward arrow.*

The anticline shown has been affected by:

*Options as printed:* A) Normal fault   B) Reverse fault   C) Thrust fault   D) Tear fault
questions.corrige_markdown:
The arrows on the front face show **vertical** movement of the two blocks (one block down, the other up) along a steep plane, so the fault is a dip-slip fault and not a tear (strike-slip) fault, which would show horizontal arrows on the top surface. A thrust is a low angle reverse fault, and the plane here is steep. The anticline itself is a product of compression, and a reverse fault is the dip-slip fault formed by the same compression, so the best reading is a reverse fault. The figure does not make the direction of dip of the plane clear, so a normal fault cannot be fully excluded.

**Intended answer: B (Reverse fault).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 3, the same block diagram as in question 26) and answer this question.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: a block with an anticline cut by a steep fault.*

The type of forces that have acted on the block are:

*Options as printed:* A) Tensional   B) Compressional   C) Distortional   D) Gravitational
questions.corrige_markdown:
An anticline is an upfold produced by horizontal **compression** of the layers, and a reverse fault is also produced by compression. The forces that have acted on the block are therefore compressional. (If the fault were a normal fault, tension would also have acted after the folding, which is why the question is not completely reliable.)

**Intended answer: B (Compressional).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The chemical reaction process that involves the addition of water into the composition of minerals is referred to as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In **hydration** water molecules are taken into the crystal structure of a mineral, which swells and changes into a hydrated mineral (for example anhydrite $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ becoming gypsum $\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O}$). Hydrolysis is a reaction between the mineral and the $\mathrm{H^+}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-}$ ions of water that produces new minerals (feldspar changing to clay), solution is plain dissolving, and a hydrothermal reaction involves hot fluids at depth.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What causes the brown coloration in basalts?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Fresh basalt is dark grey to black because of its ferromagnesian minerals (pyroxene, olivine). The brown colour appears when the iron in these minerals is **oxidized** by air and water to iron oxides and hydroxides such as hematite and limonite (rust). The mere presence of the minerals (A) gives the dark colour, and feldspars contain no iron, so they cannot make the rock brown.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solvent and chemical action of water on rocks is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Corrosion** (also called solution) is the chemical action of water on the rocks, especially the dissolving of soluble rocks such as limestone and the chemical attack of carbonic acid in river and sea water. Saltation is the bouncing of sand grains by wind or water, hydration and hydrolysis are particular chemical weathering reactions and not the general solvent action.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A steep-sided tunnel on the roof of a cliff formed by marine erosion is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **blow hole** is a narrow, steep-sided shaft that wave action cuts upwards from the roof of a sea cave through to the top of the cliff, so that spray is blown out of it. A stack is an isolated rock pillar, an arch is a bridge of rock left when a cave goes right through a headland, and a cave is the hollow at the foot of the cliff.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Chemical analysis was done on two samples of sandstone J and K and the following results were obtained: J = 30% quartz, 45% rock fragment, 25% feldspar; K = 30% quartz, 15% rock fragment, 55% feldspar. Use this information to answer questions 32 and 33.

Identify specimen K.
questions.corrige_markdown:
K contains 55 % feldspar, more than quartz (30 %) and rock fragments (15 %). A sandstone in which feldspar is the main constituent is an **arkose**. Orthoquartzite is almost pure quartz, a lithic sandstone is rich in rock fragments and a greywacke is a dark sandstone with a clay matrix.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Chemical analysis was done on two samples of sandstone J and K and the following results were obtained: J = 30% quartz, 45% rock fragment, 25% feldspar; K = 30% quartz, 15% rock fragment, 55% feldspar. Use this information to answer questions 32 and 33.

Name the environment of formation of J.

*Options as printed:* A) Arid   B) Geosyncline   C) Shallow marine   D) Deep marine
questions.corrige_markdown:
J contains 45 % rock fragments, more than quartz or feldspar, so it is a **lithic sandstone** (litharenite). This is an immature sandstone: it is made of unweathered fragments eroded from rising mountain belts and dumped quickly into a rapidly subsiding trough next to them, which is the geosynclinal setting. Arkose (K) forms in arid or semi-arid climates and orthoquartzite in stable shallow marine settings. The link between a lithic sandstone and one single environment is not unique (turbidite deposits of deep marine troughs are also lithic), so the question is not fully reliable.

**Intended answer: B (Geosyncline).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Name the type of sedimentary rock commonly formed around reefs.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Reefs are built by corals, calcareous algae and shell-forming organisms in warm, clear, shallow sea water, so the rock formed around them is made of calcium carbonate: **limestone** (reef limestone). Shale and mudstone form from mud in quiet water and sandstone from sand.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Name an argillaceous rock which is composed of silts and is fissile.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Argillaceous rocks are the clay-rich, fine grained sedimentary rocks. Among them **shale** is the one that is made of silt and clay and is **fissile**, which means that it splits easily into thin sheets along the bedding. Mudstone and claystone are similar rocks but are massive (not fissile), and siltstone is not argillaceous (it is made mainly of silt grains and is not clay-rich).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: State the environment where conglomerate will not likely be formed.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A conglomerate is made of rounded pebbles, which need strong water currents to transport and round them: they accumulate in river channels (fluvial), on beaches (littoral) and as basal deposits of shallow seas that advance over the land. In a **desert** the wind moves only sand and finer grains, which build dunes and give sandstones; gravel is left behind as a lag and is rarely buried to make a conglomerate (the exception being the occasional fan deposits of flash floods).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 4) and answer questions 37, 38 and 39.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: a trilobite seen from above. A broad rim with fine radial lines surrounds the head (cephalon), which has a swollen central glabella and two long spines running backwards; the part marked W is pointed to by a label line.*

Identify the trilobite.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The head of the trilobite has a broad rim with radial pits (a fringe), a swollen club-shaped glabella, no eyes and long genal spines trailing backwards, with a short thorax and a small tail. These are the features of **Trinucleus**. Paradoxides is large with a long glabella and big spines, Illaenus is smooth with an almost featureless head and tail, and Dalmanites has large eyes and a spiny tail.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 4, the trilobite of question 37) and answer this question.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: a trilobite seen from above. A broad rim with fine radial lines surrounds the head (cephalon), which has a swollen central glabella and two long spines running backwards; the part marked W is pointed to by a label line.*

Name the part labeled W.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The label W points to the wide outer rim of the head carrying radial lines or pits. In Trinucleus this rim is the **fringe**, a diagnostic feature of the genus. The fixed cheek is one of the two lobes beside the glabella (the rounded areas inside the rim), the head is the whole cephalon and the cephalic margin is only the outer edge.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 4, the trilobite of question 37) and answer this question.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: a trilobite seen from above. A broad rim with fine radial lines surrounds the head (cephalon), which has a swollen central glabella and two long spines running backwards; the part marked W is pointed to by a label line.*

State the mode of life of this trilobite.

*Options as printed:* A) Floater   B) Crawler   C) Burrower   D) Swimmer.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Trinucleus was blind and lived on or just in the soft muddy sea floor in rather deep water. It had a flat, broad fringed head and a small body, and it is usually classified as a bottom-dwelling (benthonic) **crawler** or scavenger. Some authors suggest that it lay partly buried in the mud, so the usual classification into crawler or burrower is not unique and the printed key cannot be known with certainty.

**Intended answer: B (Crawler).**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A dendroid coral having massive corallites is:

*Options as printed:* A) Phaceloid   B) Ceroid   C) Astracoid   D) Isastrea
questions.corrige_markdown:
Colonial corals are classified by the way the corallites (the individual cups) are arranged. In a **phaceloid** colony the corallites are long, cylindrical and separate, like a bush or tree, which is the dendroid type of growth. In ceroid and astraeoid colonies the corallites are joined in a solid mass and Isastrea is a genus (a massive coral) and not a growth form. The phrase "dendroid coral having massive corallites" mixes terms, so the printed question is not reliable.

**Intended answer: A (Phaceloid).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: How can you differentiate between a planispirally coiled gastropod shell and an ammonoid shell?
questions.corrige_markdown:
An ammonoid shell is divided by walls called **septa** into chambers, and a tube called the **siphuncle** runs through the chambers; the animal lives in the last chamber. A gastropod shell is a single, continuous tube, without septa, chambers or a siphuncle. Only option C states this correctly; A, B and D give the features to the wrong group.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Gastropod shell has chambers, ammonoid shell does not.
Ammonoid shell lacks septa, gastropod shell has septa.
Gastropod shell does not have siphuncle and lacks septa, ammonoid shell has siphuncle and is divided into chambers and has septa.
Ammonoid shell is not divided into chambers and lacks septa, gastropod shell is divided into chambers and has septa.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the rock sequence below (Figure 5) and answer questions 42 and 43.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: a sketch of a rock section with horizontal beds (shale, limestone and conglomerate), a vertical dyke through the middle and a sloping line F with a layered block above it.*

Which stratigraphic principle represents the relationship between the dyke and the surrounding rocks?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The dyke is an igneous body that cuts across the beds of shale, limestone and conglomerate. By the principle of **cross-cutting relationships** a feature that cuts across another is younger than the rock it cuts, so the dyke is younger than the beds that it intrudes. Superposition and original horizontality apply to the order of the layers and uniformitarianism is the general principle "the present is the key to the past".

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the rock sequence below (Figure 5, the same section as in question 42) and answer this question.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: a rock section with a vertical dyke cut by the sloping line F.*

Name the type of fault shown.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sloping line F dips down to the left. The vertical dyke is displaced by it: the upper part of the dyke (in the block above the fault, the hanging wall) lies further to the left than the lower part. The hanging wall has therefore moved down the dip of the fault, which is the movement of a **normal fault** (a reverse or thrust fault would push the hanging wall up the dip and shift the upper part of the dyke to the right). A tear fault has horizontal movement. The sketch is rough, so this reading rests on the offset of the dyke.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which event leads to the deposition of rocks with a fining upwards sequence?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a **transgression** the sea moves over the land, so the water becomes deeper with time at any one place. Coarse shoreline sediments (conglomerate, sandstone) are covered by finer and finer ones (siltstone, shale, limestone), so the sequence fines upwards. In a regression the shoreline retreats, water becomes shallower and the sequence coarsens upwards. Cyclic and rhythmic sedimentation describe repeated alternations and are not by themselves a cause of fining upwards.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the sketch map (Figure 6) and answer questions 45 and 46.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: a sketch geological map with a key (sandstone, conglomerate; limestone, sandstone, sandy limestone, shale) showing one group of beds with dip marks truncated by another group of beds with a different direction.*

The type of unconformity shown is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
On the map the older group of beds (limestone, sandstone, sandy limestone, shale) has a strike and dip that are different from those of the younger beds (sandstone and conglomerate) lying across them. Beds which are not parallel on the two sides of the unconformity surface mean that the older beds were tilted and eroded before the younger beds were laid down: this is an **angular unconformity**. In parallel unconformities and disconformities the beds on both sides have the same orientation.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the sketch map (Figure 6, the same map as in question 45) and answer this question.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2019-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: a sketch geological map with a key of the rock types.*

Name one evidence that can be used to identify the unconformity on the map.
questions.corrige_markdown:
On a geological map an unconformity shows where the outcrop boundaries of the older beds **end abruptly** against the surface of the younger beds, because the older beds were tilted and eroded before the younger ones were deposited. A dip direction (B), the order of beds with the oldest at the bottom (C, true for any sequence) and a change of dip value (D, which also happens across a fold or a fault) are not specific to an unconformity.

**Answer: A.**

Older beds are at the bottom and younger beds are at the top.

questions.enonce_markdown: An area in the crust where hot mantle plumes rise is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A mantle plume is a column of unusually hot rock that rises from deep in the mantle and melts under the crust, forming a **hot spot** (for example Hawaii and the Cameroon Volcanic Line). A rift valley is a down-dropped block between faults, a volcano is a surface landform and the epicentre is the point on the surface above an earthquake focus.

**Answer: D.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the name of the failed arm of a tripple junction?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Continental rifting often begins above a hot spot with three rifts that meet at about $120^\circ$ (a triple junction). Two arms open into an ocean, while the third stops spreading: this is the failed arm, or **aulacogen** (the Benue Trough of Nigeria is an example). A Benioff zone is the inclined earthquake zone of a subduction zone and a transcurrent fault is a strike-slip fault.

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: Where are hydrothermal deposits usually found?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hydrothermal deposits are formed when hot, mineral-rich water from a cooling magma moves through the surrounding rocks and deposits minerals as it cools. The fluid follows fractures and joints, so the minerals (quartz and the ores of gold, copper, lead, zinc and tin) are deposited as **veins inside cracks**. The deposits can be found at different distances from the intrusion (the more soluble minerals travel farther), so only option C applies to them all.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: A distance away from the intrusion

questions.enonce_markdown: Name the type of springs common with fractured rocks?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In rocks with a network of joints and fractures, water moves down along the cracks and comes out where a joint or fracture meets the surface: these are **joint springs** (fracture springs). Dyke springs are held up by a dyke, contact springs occur where a permeable bed lies on an impermeable one, and hot springs are heated by volcanic activity.

**Answer: A.**
